clue.text: Heroic tale the writer of Bonjour Tristesse left unfinished

indicators.note: a word left unfinished loses its final letter, so the novelist's surname is cut short

parts.note: Françoise Sagan wrote the 1954 novel Bonjour Tristesse

explanation.surface: A heroic story that the French novelist never got round to finishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A Norse or Icelandic prose epic of heroes and feuds is the original example of this kind of story.

clue.text: It's drunk in a day, up to the time of a party

parts.note: Mon is the standard abbreviation for Monday
till means until, up to a given time
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Someone gets drunk in a single day, right up to the start of a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's drunk' looks like a description of a reveller, but it defines the drink itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This medium-dry Spanish sherry is a beverage, so it is something that gets drunk.

clue.text: Possibly she's at our bookshop signing

definitions.text: Possibly she's at our bookshop signing

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman writer might well be found signing copies at our local bookshop.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a female writer could be at the bookshop signing her books.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who writes books is the sort of person who appears at a shop to sign copies of them.

clue.text: Childhood friend taking coach to match

parts.note: to school someone is to coach or train them
to mate is to pair or match one thing with another

explanation.surface: A friend from one's early years is taken along to a sports fixture by coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' and 'match' suggest a bus and a game, but they are both verbs here.
explanation.definitionFit: A classmate from one's school days is a friend made during childhood.

clue.text: Doubter takes a lot of flak for pinching mushroom

indicators.note: pinching means grabbing hold of, so one piece holds the other inside it
a lot of a word, but not all, means dropping its final letter

parts.note: stick is informal for criticism or flak, as in 'taking stick'
a cep is an edible mushroom, the porcini

explanation.surface: A doubter gets heavily criticised for stealing a mushroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' trims STICK to STIC, which then holds CEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who doubts accepted claims is a sceptic, the British spelling of skeptic.

clue.text: One may accommodate aspirants, to a degree

definitions.text: One may accommodate aspirants, to a degree

parts.words: One may accommodate aspirants, to a degree
parts.note: the aspirants are students working towards a university degree, and the building houses them

explanation.surface: Something gives a measure of room to ambitious people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to a degree' looks like 'somewhat', but it means aspiring to a university degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A university building where students live while studying for their degrees.

clue.text: 39 books were sufficient for an old Roman port

parts.note: the Old Testament, abbreviated OT, has 39 books in the Protestant canon
ran to means stretched to or was enough to cover, as money runs to something

explanation.surface: Thirty-nine volumes were enough to cover an ancient Roman harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: '39' is no clue reference but the count of books in the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: The town in Apulia, Italy, was the Roman harbour Hydruntum, an ancient port on the Adriatic.

clue.text: Sound young Shakespearean lord dismissing clan leaders?

indicators.note: dismissing means sending away, so letters are removed from the name

parts.note: Claudio is the young lord of Florence in Much Ado About Nothing

indicators.note: the leaders of a word are its opening letters, here both C and L

explanation.surface: A young Shakespearean nobleman sends away the chiefs of a Scottish clan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders' takes the first letters of 'clan', CL, which come off the front of CLAUDIO.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, audio means relating to sound, as in audio equipment.

clue.text: Lofty dwelling built by first of yachtsmen in lake

indicators.note: in signals one piece placed inside another

parts.note: Erie is one of the North American Great Lakes

indicators.note: first of picks out the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A high-up home constructed by the leading yachtsman on a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle's nest built high on a crag, and by extension any lofty home.

clue.text: Composer reportedly bitten by scoundrel's dog

indicators.note: something bitten by another is held between its jaws, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a rotter is a scoundrel or cad

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so the composer's name is taken by its sound

parts.note: Kurt Weill composed The Threepenny Opera

explanation.surface: A composer is reported to have been bitten by a villain's dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' gives WEIL, the sound of the composer's name, which goes inside ROTTER, broken after ROTT.
explanation.definitionFit: A Rottweiler is a large, powerful German breed of dog.

clue.text: Good years regularly yielding flowing water

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is taken

explanation.surface: A run of good years produces running water.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of 'Good years' gives the river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is flowing water, and the Oder runs along the German–Polish border.

clue.text: Ultimate extremes of upset doctors treated originally

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor; MOS is the plural

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Upset doctors treated at the very limits of their endurance.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean greatest or furthest, the highest degree possible.

clue.text: Northern chap in Cockney's house, one who'll eat anything

indicators.note: in signals one piece placed inside another

parts.note: a Cockney drops the h, so home becomes 'ome
Ivor is a man's name, standing for any chap

explanation.surface: A man from the north staying in a Londoner's home will eat whatever is served.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner, famous for dropping the h.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal or person that feeds on both plants and meat, and so on anything.

clue.text: Bring round cruets — tea is prepared

indicators.note: prepared means made ready or worked into shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A host brings the cruet set to the table while the tea is being made.
explanation.definitionFit: To revive someone who has fainted is to bring them round.

clue.text: Solitary workman ultimately abandoned plant

indicators.note: abandoned means given up, so a letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: alone means solitary, on one's own

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A lone labourer is finally left on his own, plant and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives N, the last letter of 'workman', which drops out of ALONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloe is a succulent plant, as in aloe vera.

clue.text: Low vehicle with nothing on it running over pole?

parts.note: a cart is a simple vehicle
O, the figure zero, means nothing

indicators.note: running over means spanning or covering, so one piece stretches round the other

parts.note: S stands for the South Pole

explanation.surface: A low-slung vehicle carrying nothing runs over a pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like an adjective for the vehicle, but it is David Low, the famous New Zealand-born political cartoonist of the London Evening Standard.
explanation.definitionFit: David Low drew political cartoons, so he is an example of this kind of artist, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Short walk in no state to be used after dark

indicators.note: in signals one piece placed inside another

parts.note: Cal is an abbreviation for California, a US state
a turn is a short stroll, as in taking a turn round the garden

explanation.surface: Someone is in no fit state for a short walk once it gets dark.
explanation.walkthrough: TURN goes inside NOCAL, between the C and the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Nocturnal means active or occurring at night, so happening after dark.

clue.text: Old prison mother must visit, some say

indicators.note: some say means as it is spoken, so the phrase is taken by its sound

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother; shall see stands for must visit, as in 'Ma shall see'

explanation.surface: Mother has to make a trip to a prison, so people report.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marshalsea was a notorious debtors' prison in Southwark, London, where Dickens's father was held; 'Ma shall see' said in a non-rhotic accent gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marshalsea was a historic London prison, closed in 1842.

clue.text: Physical structure of a cat in a US city

indicators.note: in signals one piece placed inside another

parts.note: NY is the abbreviation for New York
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: Something describes the body shape of a cat living in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: A TOM goes inside A NY, between the N and the Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomy is the bodily structure of a living thing.

clue.text: Given a turn, as a door handle may be?

definitions.meaning: to be given a turn is to be startled or frightened

definitions.text: as a door handle may be
definitions.meaning: a door handle can be fitted with an alarm, making it wired to warn of intruders

explanation.walkthrough: 'Given a turn' looks like something done to a handle, but it means scared.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frightened means being alarmed, and a handle fitted with a warning device is alarmed too.

clue.text: Select players for fling

definitions.meaning: to choose the actors for a play or film
to throw, as a fisherman throws a line

explanation.definitionFit: To pick performers for a production and to throw something both use the same verb.

clue.text: Girl enthralled by 007?

parts.note: enthralled can mean enslaved, so this is a slave girl, and read playfully a maid in thrall to the agent 007

explanation.surface: A young woman is captivated by James Bond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enthralled' looks like 'charmed', but its old sense is held in bondage.
explanation.definitionFit: A slave girl or female servant bound to serve a master.

clue.text: Phoney press employee accepts advance, given rise

indicators.note: given rise means lifted, which in a down clue turns the letters upside down
accepts means takes in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a sub, short for sub-editor, works at a newspaper
go means advance or move forward

explanation.surface: A fake journalist pockets an advance payment and gets a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepts' puts GO inside SUB to make SUGOB; 'given rise' reverses it, reading upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Phoney and bogus both mean fake or not genuine.

clue.text: Egg on soldiers making gunpowder ingredient

indicators.note: on means on top of, so in this down clue the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a nit is the egg of a louse
RE, the Royal Engineers, is a corps of soldiers

explanation.surface: A commander urges troops on to make gunpowder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egg on' looks like 'urge', but 'Egg' is a louse's egg and 'on' places it above the soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitre, potassium nitrate or saltpetre, is the main ingredient of gunpowder.

clue.text: A Greek character twice identifying an Egyptian god

parts.note: nu is the thirteenth letter of the Greek alphabet
bis is Latin for twice, as called out for an encore

explanation.surface: A Greek letter appears twice and points to an Egyptian deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Anubis is the jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead.

clue.text: Girl in black perhaps secured husband

parts.note: got means secured or obtained
H is the abbreviation for husband in family trees

explanation.surface: A woman dressed in black has got herself a husband.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of the subculture known for black clothes and dark make-up.

clue.text: Decorative lantern a Moor oddly misused

indicators.note: misused means put to wrong use, so these letters are rearranged
oddly takes the letters in odd positions, first and third

explanation.surface: A Moor clumsily mishandles an ornate lantern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' gives MO from 'Moor', which joins LANTERN and A in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental and decorative both describe something serving as adornment.

clue.text: Retired PM's point about unknown dozer

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn, so the name is turned back

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was a British Prime Minister; PEELS is his name with the possessive
y is an unknown quantity in algebra
a head is a point, as in a headland

explanation.surface: A former prime minister's point concerns something nobody knows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' turns PEELS into SLEEP; 'about' is only a link word here.
explanation.definitionFit: A drowsy person who keeps nodding off is a dozer.

clue.text: National emblem seen to collapse suddenly?

definitions.text: National emblem seen to collapse suddenly?

parts.words: National emblem seen to collapse suddenly?
parts.note: the emblem of Wales, written backwards and so turned over, gives a word meaning to collapse suddenly when it keels over

explanation.walkthrough: The Welsh emblem read backwards is KEEL, and to keel over is to collapse suddenly; the question mark flags this playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: This vegetable is the national emblem of Wales, worn on St David's Day.
